title: Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
description: SHENZHEN, CHINA - NOVEMBER 16: The skyline is lit up for the upcoming APEC Summit on November 16, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. China will host the APEC Ec
body: SHENZHEN, CHINA - NOVEMBER 16: The skyline is lit up for the upcoming APEC Summit on November 16, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. China will host the APEC Economic Leaders Summit on November 18-19. (Photo by Kevin Frayer/Getty Images)Kevin Frayer | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesSHENZHEN, China — Leaders of the U.S., China, Russia and other major Asia-Pacific economies face a series of critical issues from wars to tech security as they gather for an annual summit this week.Since the last APEC leaders' meeting, China's tensions with Japan have escalated. Barely stabilized U.S.-China relations face new tests in the wake of Washington's scrutiny of Nvidia's China chip sales. And the Iran war, now in its ninth month, is still pressuring global energy prices, while the Russia-Ukraine war has dragged on.But expectations are low for any breakthroughs. Meanwhile for Beijing, host to this year's series of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings, the multilateral gathering is yet another venue to build its global influence. Chinese President Xi Jinping met Tuesday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and the President of Vietnam To Lam. Vietnam is hosting next year's APEC meetings. Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen early Wednesday morning, where he was greeted by Chinese Politburo Standing Committee Member Cai Qi, according to Chinese state media. U.S. President Donald Trump is in the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit before heading to Shenzhen.Here's what's at stake this week:1. U.S.-China talksTrump and Xi are expected to meet alongside the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting Wednesday and Thursday. Their summit around the gathering last year in South Korea ushered in a one-year trade truce of lower tariffs and some rare earths flows, which was extended by two months, to January 2027.In this week's summit, Trump does not plan to raise the issue of Nvidia and allegations that its former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy, U.S. officials said. They said the talks would focus on implementing the trade agreement.The U.S. and China in September said they would lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from the other country, without specifying an effective date. China said this month that it would only increase purchases of U.S. agricultural products if those tariffs were lowered.However, Washington is already moving to tighten restrictions on loopholes that had given Chinese companies access to American artificial intelligence technology. So far, China's response has been to threaten countermeasures."If there is room for genuine U.S.-China cooperation this week, it's on managing risk rather than sharing advantage," said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. That could include cooperation on an artificial intelligence security hotline."Across Asia, governments under mounting pressure to pick a side will be watching Shenzhen for signs of how much room they still have to maneuver," Bhattacharya said. "Most have little appetite for a region split into two technology camps."2. Geopolitical posturingOn Thursday, Xi is set to meet with Trump and Putin, according to Beijing's official confirmation of the event, billed as the "China-Russia-U.S. Summit."It's the first-ever gathering of the three leaders, albeit with low expectations that there will be sufficient time for thorough dialogue. But the event creates the opportunity for a globally influential photo-op similar to the one that Xi, Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had on the sidelines of a China-hosted Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in September 2025. Also closely watched will be any interaction with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Last November, her comments drew Beijing's ire after indicating Tokyo would support Taiwan if the island were seriously threatened by Beijing's military.Takaichi is expected to join the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in her first trip to China since becoming prime minister. She had met Xi on the sidelines of the APEC event last year in South Korea.Attendees from other APEC economies are hoping for more signs of cooperation. Anindya Bakrie, CEO of Indonesian conglomerate Bakrie & Brothers, told CNBC that when Trump and Xi meet, the narrative is hopefully one of peace and stability. 3. TechTech issues are likely to be in heavy focus. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is set to join Trump on the Shenzhen trip. Other American executives, such as Visa CEO Ryan McInerney, joined a two-day APEC CEO Summit that kicked off Tuesday.The APEC host city, Shenzhen, has been dubbed one of China's "Silicon Valleys" and is home to Huawei and BYD. The summit organizers are also using the event to showcase local robotics startups. A slew of tech company earnings is coming out at the same time as the APEC meeting, keeping the corporate side in the spotlight as well.Nvidia released quarterly results Wednesday morning Beijing time, following a tumultuous two weeks of scrutiny that forced the chipmaker's founder Jensen Huang to resign. The company boosted its outlook and shares rose in extended trading. Shenzhen-based gaming and social media giant Tencent is set to report its quarterly earnings Wednesday evening. The company has previously noted constraints from its limited computing power.U.S.-based AI giant Anthropic is pricing its highly anticipated initial public offering this week, and expected to list on the Nasdaq Thursday Nov. 19. Its CEO Dario Amodei has urged a slowdown in AI development and warned of the risk if China does not follow suit.—CNBC's Penny Chen and Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China

title: China’s Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers ahead of his meeting with Trump and Putin
description: Chinese President Xi Jinping looks on during a bilateral meeting with Vietnam's President To Lam on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Coopera
body: Chinese President Xi Jinping looks on during a bilateral meeting with Vietnam's President To Lam on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China's Guangdong province on November 17, 2026.  Maxim Shemetov | Afp | Getty ImagesSHENZHEN, China — Chinese President Xi Jinping opened a key Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting on Wednesday with calls for removing trade and investment barriers.The leader spoke as he was expected to host Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump this week alongside the APEC CEO and Economic Leaders Summit."We should remove trade and investment barriers," Xi said via an official English translation. He said a key reason for doing so was "to promote development that is balanced." He did not mention U.S. tariffs or other specific measures. Instead, Xi cast China as a "promising land for development" for global businesses, and indicated plans for "Bay Area" cooperation. Shenzhen, home to major Chinese tech companies, is part of China's "Greater Bay Area" that includes Hong Kong and Macau. The Silicon Valley region around San Francisco is also known as the "Bay Area" in the U.S. "China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also go a step further," Xi said. He said China would "reform" rules and regulations to give foreign businesses "full manufacturing access."Chinese exports have steadily grown their share of global manufactured goods, drawing criticism from the European Union and other regions for overcapacity. The U.S. and China last year agreed to keep tariffs lower, but the world's two largest economies have yet to implement a planned $30 billion cut in duties on goods from each side. "Global growth lacks momentum," Xi noted in his speech. But he said "still global trade keeps growing against headwinds, and breakthroughs are being made in emerging technologies at a faster pace."He said the "hard questions of our times" for Asia Pacific economies is whether to open, or close, doors — and later cast opening doors as bringing "progress.""There can be no stability without security, and no security without stability," he said. Xi called for APEC members to deepen coordination in the digital economy and AI, as a way to drive regional economic growth."Unicorn companies and large AI models have emerged in large numbers and many innovations have empowered hundreds of trades and industries and reached millions of households," he said, in some of his most specific mentions of the cutting-edge technology.

title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks
description: A vial of MMR vaccine is prepared at Dr. Gary M. Kramer's pediatric office in Coral Gables, Florida, Sept. 12, 2025.Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesThe U.S.
body: A vial of MMR vaccine is prepared at Dr. Gary M. Kramer's pediatric office in Coral Gables, Florida, Sept. 12, 2025.Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesThe U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones. "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin. The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts. The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation. In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring. Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status. The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence. But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles." "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities. Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement. "We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement. In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response." "We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America. Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported. Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses. The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

title: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate election
description: Former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democratic from Alaska and US Senate candidate, during an "Alaska Forever" campaign event at the Alaska Aviation
body: Former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democratic from Alaska and US Senate candidate, during an "Alaska Forever" campaign event at the Alaska Aviation Museum in Anchorage, Alaska, US, on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Nathaniel Wilder | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesDemocratic candidate Mary Peltola won the Alaska Senate election, capping a midterm cycle that already was one of the best for Democrats in more than a half-century, the Associated Press reported Tuesday evening.Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a race that was surrounded by controversy over an independent candidate who shared his name. Peltola had faced accusations that her campaign recruited ultra-longshot candidate Dan J. Sullivan to the race to confuse voters. The Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan lost in order to conduct an investigation into whether voter confusion tainted the outcome.The Justice Department is appealing the dismissal of that civil suit. The department is also conducting a criminal investigation into the second Sullivan's decision to enter the race.Peltola's victory gives Democrats a solid majority of 56 seats in the Senate beginning in January.Democrats this cycle flipped nine Senate seats that are currently held by Republicans.That outcome, which was not considered remotely likely at the beginning of the election, came as part of a massive Democratic wave this year, which saw the party also flip majority control of the House of Representatives by a decisive margin.Alaska was the last Senate race to be called in the midterm elections. Peltola, a former House member, joins Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan as the first two Native American women elected to the Senate.The race was called two weeks after Election Day, and six days after Peltola's fellow Democrat Scott Colom pulled off perhaps the most stunning upset of the 2026 cycle by defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate race.As of 10:39 p.m. ET, Peltola had 50.1% of the vote, and Sullivan had 45.8%. Another Republican, Gerald Heikes, had 2.1% of the vote, while Daniel J. Sullivan had 1.6% of the vote.If no candidate exceeded 50% of the vote, the election would have been decided through a ranked-choice method, in which the two bottom finishers would have been eliminated, and the second choices on the ballots of voters who selected them would be allocated to the remaining two candidates."From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska," Peltola said in a statement."Over the course of this campaign I've spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table," Peltola said. "Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first."As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said. "Thank you Alaska. Let's get to work."

schema.headline: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate election

title: 'Who and what comes next': Analysts expect Nvidia investor uncertainty despite earnings beat
description: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesAnalysts expect uncertainty around Nvidia's future to linger despite another earnings beat, noting that much of the t
body: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesAnalysts expect uncertainty around Nvidia's future to linger despite another earnings beat, noting that much of the third quarter was already locked in before the turmoil that peaked in Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO.Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG. Part of that increase reflects an extra week in the fiscal fourth quarter, which Melius Research estimated accounts for $9 billion to $10 billion of the sequential jump.The company also lifted its fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%, even with China excluded from its data center compute revenue outlook."That's a team going full steam ahead, rather than just steadying the ship, and a clear signal that management believes next year can run just fine without Jensen Huang at the helm," said Josh Gilbert, eToro's lead analyst for Asia Pacific and the Middle East.Still, even with the results that he called "nothing short of astonishing", Gilbert said "investors will still be left with the uncertainty of who and what comes next."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia's latest movements.In his first statement since he resigned last week, Huang said before the results release that he was open to returning to the company. However, chair of Nvidia's board Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO.The results should help ease some concerns created by Nvidia's recent leadership turmoil, said Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello, who described the figures as "solid" and broadly in line with the firm's expectations. Colello expressed continued confidence that "the AI infrastructure buildout is real," pointing to Nvidia's shipments holding steady in the third quarter.Michael Wilson, chief investment officer and chief U.S. equity strategist at Morgan Stanley, told CNBC TV that the results were "somewhat expected," with no major drop-off in Nvidia's business anticipated in the near term and guidance remaining "pretty constructive."Wilson said AI remained a "desirable investment," with no slowdown in spending seen or expected from hyperscalers and some neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing. However, he added that investment may not continue at the pace investors expected six months ago. Nvidia is widely seen as the bellwether for the broader AI industry and spending.Gilbert shared that view, saying the AI trade can now "let out a small sigh of relief" after holding its breath for weeks. Nvidia had been "firing on all cylinders" before Huang's departure, he said, and its underlying fundamentals remained intact.He pointed to Nvidia's supply commitments, which rose to $390 billion from $279 billion in three months, as well as its Vera Rubin platform, which has already brought in $20 billion. "It's the clearest sign yet that the AI boom still has plenty of fuel in the tank," Gilbert said.Nvidia shares rose more than 5% in after-hours trading, though Gilbert said any rally is expected to meet resistance and "plenty of volatility" in the coming weeks, with the CEO search only just getting under way and investigations still playing out.New U.S. export restrictions announced this week add another wrinkle. The Commerce Department will require licenses for shipments of advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, citing the risk that they could be diverted to China.Gilbert said the direct impact on Nvidia's forecasts appears limited because its guidance already assumed no China data center revenue, while China accounted for only around 2% of sales this quarter. However, new licensing requirements for shipments to places such as Singapore and Malaysia could slow some neocloud build-outs, he said.watch nowMelius Research analyst Ben Reitzes said fiscal 2028 is when sales to countries covered by the new restrictions would be expected to decline. He interpreted Nvidia's forecast as a sign that hyperscalers will take whatever supply becomes available elsewhere. Nvidia said it is still studying the new Commerce Department rules but remains confident in its 75% growth target.Colello pointed to longer-term risks around policy, international sales and hyperscalers developing their own chips, though he said Nvidia should remain an important player as the market expands. He said investors will now be looking for the company to reaffirm its long-term outlook and show it can continue executing through the leadership transition."We're at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don't know what Nvidia's long-term leadership will look like," Colello added. "Jensen Huang's departure could create some near-term disruption, but a credible succession plan should go a long way toward steadying the ship. The next CEO will have big shoes to fill, but Nvidia's long-term opportunity does not hinge on one person."

schema.headline: 'Who and what comes next': Analysts expect Nvidia investor uncertainty despite earnings beat

title: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
description: watch nowSentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and l
body: watch nowSentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices.Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38.Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%.Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020."Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them  reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them."The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges,  including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back."In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23. title: OpenAI bugging case defendant Alfozan set for trial in January
description: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. De
body: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeA federal judge on Tuesday set Jan. 20 for the start of the trial for Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, who is accused of planting a recording device in an OpenAI conference room when he worked for the artificial intelligence company as an engineering lead.If the trial starts on that date in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, it would be after an unusually short lag since Alfozan's arrest in October. Federal criminal cases, as a rule, do not go to trial so quickly.But Alfozan's attorney, David Rizk, sought the speedy trial after complaining at a court hearing that prosecutors have been slow in turning over evidence in the case.Rizk also said prosecutors have not given him any evidence that Alfozan engaged in espionage, after they argued successfully last month that he should be detained without bail, and after saying his alleged bugging "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."Among other things, prosecutors had noted that Alfozan is a venture partner at Saudi venture firm Raed Ventures alongside a member of the Saudi royal family, Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud.Alfozan, who has pleaded not guilty in the case, is charged with one count of intercepting oral communications. He faces a maximum of five years in prison if he is convicted.Prosecutors have said Alfozan was arrested after staff at OpenAI found a recording device wrapped in toilet paper and installed in the back of a television in the conference room at its San Francisco headquarters in September. A surveillance camera captured Alfozan looking at the gadget in the room.Assistant U.S. Attorney Nick Parker told Judge Vince Chhabria on Tuesday that government investigators have been locked out of Alfozan's phone, but they have also collected one other phone, a tablet, and two laptops. Prosecutors also obtained 160 hours of recordings from meetings in a conference room. The recording device itself is encrypted, but if data was backed up to another device, investigators would have been able to obtain it, Parker said.watch nowChhabria told prosecutors that they must turn over all reports the FBI has created to Alfozan's attorney by Nov. 24, and that they must also move quickly to give the defense other evidence for use at trial."We need to make sure that you get whatever discovery you're entitled to promptly," Chhabria told Rizk.OpenAI, which fired Alfozan after his arrest, has said it lacked proof of him taking source code or customer data. Chhabria also told Parker he wants to see, within seven days, any evidence that might exist showing Alfozan carrying out economic espionage, stealing trade secrets or acting as an unregistered foreign agent. Parker said he was not aware of any such evidence at this time."At this point, I'm not suggesting the defendant stole anything," Parker said.The prosecutor told the judge that his team had a "serious concern" about Rizk's plans to review evidence turned over to the defense with an AI tool that competes with OpenAI. Parker noted that among the seized evidence is a laptop that might have proprietary OpenAI data.Chhabria replied, "I'm a lot less concerned about that than you are."The judge ordered Parker to submit a motion by Friday explaining why the defense's use of a competing AI to analyze evidence might be a problem. Rizk told CNBC he intends to use Anthropic's Claude. Anthropic, which aims to go public on Nasdaq this week, was founded by OpenAI employees.— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this report. title: Nvidia closes lower ahead of earnings as company reels from Huang resignation
description: watch nowNvidia shares closed marginally lower Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the co
body: watch nowNvidia shares closed marginally lower Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell.The stock move Tuesday marked Nvidia's fourth straight daily decline.In the statement, Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation.""If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued. Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia stock chartNvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025. Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2. Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025. An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures, including Elon Musk. But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday.The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.Read more CNBC tech newsAnthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBCDemis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEOOpenAI inks agreements with four independent evaluators to boost company’s safety workHow Rockstar’s ‘GTA VI’ release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off

title: Trump’s accounts traded up to $97.5 million in Nvidia as Huang gained White House access
description: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, left, President Donald Trump and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, right, walk back to the White House following a media
body: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, left, President Donald Trump and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, right, walk back to the White House following a media briefing after a meeting on artificial intelligence outside the White House, Sept. 29, 2026.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia.The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang, became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August. By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear.Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight.Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18, the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported.Trump on Monday denied being briefed. Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz. Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone, compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis.Read more on Trump investmentsTrump bought up to $25 million in Meta and millions in SpaceX debt in AugustTrump’s municipal bond portfolio reaches as much as $1 billion as policy overlaps mountTrump disclosure shows 1,100 July trades, Microsoft and Amazon salesTrump’s oil investments have gained millions during Iran war as his accounts keep tradingTrump’s foreign licensing business booms to $59.5 million as Gulf developers payJPMorgan, Schwab and UBS manage millions in Trump’s $858 million investment portfolioTrump bought as much as $5 million in Axon stock before ICE sought $220 million Taser dealCompany that bet big on Trump-backed crypto says its fortunes have improvedTrump family got about $500M from crypto venture — but investors saw steep lossesTrump Jr. calls banking a 'Ponzi scheme' that forced family to create crypto businessThe Trump family crypto empire looks to Asia: Eric Trump talks Bitcoin in Hong KongTrump family says U.S. dollar needs an upgrade and they are the ones to do itA White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence.Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war."Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses.Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance.Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street. The two have met or appeared together at least 15 times since Trump returned to office, according to a CNBC review of public records and news reports. Huang in June told The Associated Press that Trump even "calls me in the middle of the night."It wasn't always that way.At Trump's Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration, several Silicon Valley titans occupied prime seats, but Huang wasn't there. The two men had never met.That changed on Jan. 31, 2025, when Huang visited the White House, capping a bruising week for Nvidia: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek had wiped $593 billion off the company's market value in a single day, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.Two days before the meeting, Trump's money managers bought between $1 million and $5 million in Nvidia stock. For Huang, much of the relationship hinged on access to China. In April 2025, the administration effectively halted sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China, prompting a $4.5 billion charge, according to an SEC filing. Huang argued that withholding U.S. chips would only accelerate China's development of its own.The administration eventually relented. After another meeting with Trump in July 2025, Huang announced from Beijing that Nvidia expected to resume H20 sales. A week after Trump confirmed an August 2025 deal calling for 15% of the revenue from the company's chip sales to China to go to the U.S. government, his accounts also bought between $5 million and $25 million in Nvidia stock, one of several large tech investments that day.Huang was also becoming a fixture of Trump's international diplomacy, joining him in Saudi Arabia and the U.K. Nvidia, already a $1 million donor to Trump's inaugural fund, would pledge another $25 million to his planned White House ballroom on condition of anonymity, The Washington Post first reported.But behind the scenes, intelligence officials first briefed Trump last fall on Huang's relationship with the woman suspected of spying for China, The New York Times reported.Trump nevertheless continued to ease restrictions on Nvidia's business in China, announcing Dec. 8 that the company could sell its more powerful H200 chips. His accounts had sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock four days earlier and bought more the day after.In the first eight months of 2026, Trump's accounts made another 38 Nvidia trades worth a combined $9.4 million to $28.3 million, according to CNBC's analysis. A disclosure released Oct. 8 — the day Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science — showed purchases of up to $1.6 million and sales of up to $1 million in August alone.Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia's board weighed his future last week, urging him to fight to keep his job, the Times reported. With Huang out and Nvidia's shares tumbling, Trump described him Thursday as a "tremendous talent" who was "going through hell" — in the same interview in which he boasted of the market's record highs.Trump is already floating a comeback for Huang, telling reporters Monday that reinstating him "certainly isn't a bad idea." But Nvidia's board is not considering his return, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because they were discussing internal matters."

schema.headline: Trump’s accounts traded up to $97.5 million in Nvidia as Huang gained White House access

title: Trump on Iran's reported DC dirty bomb plan: 'We take it very seriously'
description: President Donald Trump attends a multilateral meeting with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel in Manila, Philippines, No
body: President Donald Trump attends a multilateral meeting with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel in Manila, Philippines, Nov. 17, 2026.Win McNamee | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump said Tuesday that if a report about Iran developing plans to target top administration officials with a "dirty bomb" in Washington is true, Iran would face consequences."Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before," Trump said when asked if there is any imminent threat to Washington, home to close to 700,000 people in addition to the seat of government."I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously, because they happen to be crazy," Trump said during a photo op with world leaders at the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila, Philippines. "This is why they can't have a nuclear weapon, by the way, in case people had any questions," Trump added, reiterating his main rationale for launching a war with Iran in late February.Late Monday, CNN cited two U.S. officials in reporting that new U.S. intelligence has intercepted "very specific" plans, including "locations and targets," related to a potential Iranian plot to set off a dirty bomb, which combines conventional explosives with radioactive material.Officials have debated whether Iran would actually attempt to detonate such a device in the U.S., or even if it could, CNN reported, citing seven U.S. officials in total. CNBC has not verified the report. Trump administration spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CNN in a statement that the U.S. is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."Trump was asked about imminent Iranian threats during the first leg of his tour through Asia, which began at ASEAN and is set to include high-stakes meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.watch nowAsked about the dirty bomb report on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Tuesday morning, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested the Iranian plot was not new and described Tehran as "aspirational" in its threats. If Iran were to take such an action, "you would cause an all-out war" with the U.S., which would attack at such a level that the Islamic Republic's allies, such as China and Russia, would not come to its aid, Mullin said.It is a threat, and "we take it very serious," he said. "But the homeland is secure, I can tell you that. But every day we addressing new threats."CNN reported later Tuesday morning that NSA Net, the classified communications network used by the National Security Agency, is down, citing six people familiar with the matter.

schema.headline: Trump on Iran's reported DC dirty bomb plan: 'We take it very seriously'

title: LeBron James sues startup over viral AI ad allegedly exploiting his likeness
description: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 15: LeBron James #23 of the Philadelphia 76ers dribbles the ball against the Indiana Pacers at Xfinity Mobile Ar
body: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 15: LeBron James #23 of the Philadelphia 76ers dribbles the ball against the Indiana Pacers at Xfinity Mobile Arena on November 15, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images)Mitchell Leff | Getty Images Sport | Getty ImagesNBA superstar LeBron James sued artificial intelligence-powered sports betting startup Bron and its two founders, accusing them of using his name, likeness and AI-generated voice without permission to promote their app.In a lawsuit filed Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, James accused PlayVision, which operates the Bron app, and co-founders Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby of deliberately exploiting his "Bron" nickname to mislead consumers into believing he endorsed or was affiliated with the app.The complaint alleges that the startup released an AI-generated advertisement earlier this month depicting James in a basketball locker room, wearing a jersey bearing his nickname and the iconic number 23, along with his tattoos and a simulated version of his voice. The video showed the AI-generated figure scrolling through NBA betting options on the app.James alleged that the defendants deliberately sought to provoke controversy to generate publicity for their app, with the advertisement attracting about one million views on X within a day. The lawsuit claims the founders calculated that the publicity would outweigh any potential legal consequences, effectively treating the alleged violation of James' rights as a marketing expense. It argues that James' endorsements are "uniquely valuable," adding, "That is why defendants decided to steal it for themselves."The NBA star's lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter on Nov. 5, after which the startup removed the ad from its X and Instagram accounts and said it was working to change the app's name, according to the complaint. However, the ad remained available through third-party reposts, and the company had not changed the app's name as of the lawsuit's filing.James is seeking damages and a court order preventing the defendants from using his name, image, likeness, and voice, as well as the Bron name.Bron, operated by PlayVision, is described in Apple's App Store as a "sports analytics and betting research app with live odds comparisons, data-backed picks, player and team trends, a multi-leg Slip and bet tracking." The listing says it does not accept wagers. PlayVision is headquartered in California and participated in Y Combinator's fall 2025 batch.— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this story.

title: Widespread outages hit banks, air travel, the NSA and Apple, disrupting seemingly everything
description: watch nowDirector of National Intelligence Jay Clayton dismissed suspicions that malicious activity led to a series of outages at major tech firms and
body: watch nowDirector of National Intelligence Jay Clayton dismissed suspicions that malicious activity led to a series of outages at major tech firms and government agencies over the past week. "This is not cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state," he told CNBC's "Closing Bell" on Tuesday. "We've looked very closely." It's been a tough few days for the technology world after a series of widespread disruptions brought different parts of life to a halt.On Tuesday, an outage halted internal communications at the National Security Agency, and iPhone maker Apple confirmed that different products were either down or having issues.The NSA pointed to "scheduled routine maintenance," while Apple cited "an internal update" as the reason behind its issues.It marked four major system problems in four consecutive business days.watch nowMicrosoft's Outlook issues wreaked havoc on businesses on Thursday, and the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights on Friday. On Monday, issues at JPMorgan Chase affected customer transactions, and an outage at United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights. "When Microsoft goes down, the whole world comes to a standstill," said Raj Rajamani, CEO of JetStream Security. "That's a stark reminder of how deeply embedded these services and technologies are in our day-to-day life."The disruptions have rattled consumers and led to a steady stream of memes on social media, as people look for a silver lining — or sinister plot — in the string of technology problems.Experts say the real culprit behind this strange series of coincidences is much more benign."We're in the weird teenage phase of technology not quite maturing enough to know how to do this without disrupting services and so forth," said Tom Hegel, research head at SentinelOne.Read more CNBC tech newsAnthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBCDemis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEOOpenAI inks agreements with four independent evaluators to boost company’s safety workHow Rockstar’s ‘GTA VI’ release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time offWith the help of artificial intelligence, businesses are patching more software vulnerabilities than ever before and updating archaic systems to prepare for swarms of attacks in the wake of high-profile incidents like Hugging Face. That's leaving information technology and security teams strained and scrambling to keep up with heightened demand, said Sam Rubin, senior vice president of consulting and threat intelligence at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42.Amid this prolonged period of uncertainty, Rubin said businesses should prioritize updating their most exploitable systems and keeping operations underway when an outage hits."You need to think about how you continue to operate in the face of one of your IT systems going down," he said.Clayton told CNBC that routine upgrades are commonplace at any organization and called for a nationwide digital infrastructure upgrade.Last week, millions of users lost access to email in a fiasco that Microsoft eventually said was the result of an undetected bug that was lurking since July. The FAA, which is still looking into the root cause of its system failure, pointed in part to a router upgrade in southern Arkansas overseen by government contractor L3Harris Technologies that overwhelmed the agency's telecommunications network. JPMorgan said longer-than-usual service times on Monday stemmed from a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.Agencies and businesses have ruled out cyberattacks, but the routine patching alibi hasn't satisfied some skeptics, and lawmakers are calling for more transparency.Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., on Tuesday used the recent incidents to make the case for an AI safety bill. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., acknowledged that it's "too premature" to conclude malicious activity but called for a congressional briefing."I think it's time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken and we can inform the people of the United States of America," he said during a press conference on Tuesday.watch now

title: Japan exports in October surge 20.5%, beating estimates on robust chip shipments
description: Employees move semiconductor testers on the assembly line of the Advantest Corp. plant in Ora, Japan on Aug. 10, 2012.Tomohiro Ohsumi | Bloomberg | Ge
body: Employees move semiconductor testers on the assembly line of the Advantest Corp. plant in Ora, Japan on Aug. 10, 2012.Tomohiro Ohsumi | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesJapan's exports in October surged 20.5% from a year earlier, snapping a two-month slowdown in shipments, official data released Wednesday showed.Exports growth beat expectations of economists polled by Reuters that had pegged it at 20%, and it was sharply higher compared to a revised 16.5% in September. Shipments of semiconductor equipment that have been propping up Tokyo's exports jumped 49.7% by value. Exports of motor vehicles climbed 19.9% year on year. In terms of destinations, shipments to China rose 13.3%, while they climbed 23.9% to the U.S. Exports have been the main driver of Japan's growth, although a surge in the value of imports of petroleum due to the Iran war has offset some the impact of the exports surge on its economy. Import growth in Japan for October came in at 21.6%, sharply missing analysts' estimates of 25.8%, with petroleum imports climbing 60.5% by value, even as volumes slipped 0.7%. Analysts previously told CNBC that the surge in value was because Japan was attempting to switch sources to more expensive American oil as shipments from the Middle East stalled.Imports of petroleum from the U.S. jumped more than 1,100% year on year by value and 738% by volume. In contrast, shipments from the Middle East dipped 16.5% by volume, while higher prices pushed up import value by 37.7%. The country posted a surprise contraction in its third quarter GDP, which shrank 0.1% on an annualized basis.Following the data, Japan's Nikkei 225 was up 0.91%, while the yen traded at 159.50 to the dollar. title: Wall Street's fear gauge is surging again and this time it's not just about AI jitters
description: Traders work at the New York Stock Exchange on Nov. 17, 2026. NYSEThere's a bull market... in fear.Faced with a barrage of headlines from nationwide t
body: Traders work at the New York Stock Exchange on Nov. 17, 2026. NYSEThere's a bull market... in fear.Faced with a barrage of headlines from nationwide tech outages to Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's initial public offering, traders on Tuesday piled into protective put options on the S&P 500 Index at a rate that suggests fear beyond just an AI-specific correction.The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) surged nearly 5 points to a high of 27.7 at the worst of Tuesday's selling and the ratio of put to call volumes on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) hit 1.5, the highest since the first week of April, according to Barchart data. The 'VIX' was last still hovering above 26.With the VIX climbing four days in a row, the volatility gauge hasn't traded under 16 since Oct. 16, arguably trending higher as the S&P 500 slips below this month's lows, trading under 7,300 for the lowest price for the benchmark equity gauge since June. Cboe's three-month volatility gauge, VIX3M, briefly touched the highest since April.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCboe Volatility Index, YTDWhile Nvidia earnings are contributing to the uncertainty – the stock's options currently imply more than a 7% move after its report, the biggest in almost two years – volatility in the S&P 500 jumped more than in the Nasdaq 100 Tuesday, pointing to a more widespread fear among investors."SPX vol is expanding faster than NDX vol, as SPX vol is coming from a lower base," Eric Metz, CIO, SpiderRock Advisors for BlackRock, said via email. "Today, the market is pricing acute near-term stress in large-caps broadly, but tech-specific fear is still notable.Even within the technology cohort, Tuesday's laggards took on a different tone. Software stocks declined the most ahead of Anthropic's IPO, with options volume on the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) surging to almost four times the 30-day average, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Salesforce was hardest hit, with put contracts outpacing calls on twice the average options volume."There's a lot of reasons to be risk-off," said Noel Smith, co-CIO of Kai Asset Management. "This is a market-wide phenomenon today that's not just AI stocks."To be sure, bulls weren't totally absent from the session, with the Nasdaq 100 Index holding its November low and VIX still under its Nov. 5 high of 28.4."While vol is now at a relatively elevated level, we have not seen much fear in the options market," said VolSignals' Matthew Nadel, citing fixed-strike volatility in S&P 500 options, which measures volatility changes across specific options strikes. "We have seen a pretty decent move higher in SPX fixed strike vol, however the move up in vol has been mostly orderly."

schema.headline: Wall Street's fear gauge is surging again and this time it's not just about AI jitters
